We started the meal calendar because Sunday dinner had become a scramble, and nobody knew whether Grandma was bringing food or just coming to eat. The calendar is for the next six weeks, from October 7 through November 17, and it covers Sunday dinner plus two weekday meals each week. My sister Lena offered to keep the shared copy on the refrigerator, and I said I could enter changes on my phone after people texted her. We are not changing the old family rule that nobody has to cook on their birthday, and the calendar is only a plan, not a promise.

At the first kitchen meeting, we had six people around the table: Grandma Jo, Aunt Priya, Lena, my brother Marcus, my daughter Ellie, and me. Marcus brought the paper calendar from the pharmacy, and Ellie drew a small leaf beside each Sunday so the kids could see which meal was coming up. Grandma said, “I can make the soup, but only if somebody else carries the big pot.” We all agreed that was fair. The first meeting was on Tuesday—no, Thursday, October 3—because Marcus had written the wrong day in his message. I put Thursday in the notes and changed the calendar before anyone copied it.

We picked the first Sunday meal as lentil soup, bread, and salad at Grandma Jo’s apartment. Lena will bring the bread from the bakery on Pine Street, and I will take the soup pot upstairs because the elevator is slow and the pot is heavy. Ellie asked whether soup counted as a full meal, and Grandma said, “Right,” meaning yes, it does if we also have bread and something fresh. Marcus offered to bring salad, but he cannot shop before six on weekdays, so that offer is only for Sunday. The salad can be whatever greens look good, and we do not need to buy a particular kind.

Then I read out the weekday plan and asked everyone to stop me if a date would not work:
1. On Monday, October 7, Marcus will make chicken rice bowls at his place and set aside one plain bowl for Ellie because she does not want the sauce.
2. On Wednesday, October 9, I will make baked potatoes at home, and people can add beans, cheese, or broccoli.
3. On Monday, October 14, Lena will bring vegetable noodles to Grandma’s, and she will text before leaving so Grandma can meet her at the front door.
4. On Wednesday, October 16, Aunt Priya will make eggplant with couscous, but only if she finds the mild paprika she uses. If the shop has only the hot kind, she will message the group, and we will move that meal to the following Wednesday.
5. On Monday, October 21, there is no shared meal because Marcus has a late shift, and everyone can sort out dinner for themselves.
6. On Wednesday, October 23, Ellie and I will make tomato pasta together at our apartment, and we will keep the cheese in a separate bowl.

After that, we filled in the next two Sundays and checked the family calendar on the wall against the messages on Lena’s phone. Sunday, October 13, is roasted chicken at Aunt Priya’s, and she asked us to arrive at 5:30 rather than 6:00 because her building is testing the fire alarm at 7:00. Sunday, October 20, is chili at my place. I will make one pot with beans and a second, smaller pot without beans for Grandma Jo because beans upset her stomach. Lena said she could bring cornbread, but she has not chosen a bakery yet, so the note just says “cornbread if available.” I asked whether that meant we should buy some if she could not find it, and she said yes, we should keep a small loaf in the freezer as a backup.

We still entered the dates so nobody would assume those weeks were forgotten. Sunday, October 27, is marked “soup or stew at Grandma’s,” with the cook to be chosen after Marcus gets his schedule. Sunday, November 3, is marked “family leftovers at my place,” and everybody should bring one labeled container if they want to share. Monday, November 4, is a possible meal at Lena’s, but only if she is not working the late shift that day. If she is working late, the meal moves to Wednesday, November 6, and I will update the wall calendar once she confirms. Sunday, November 10, is marked lunch rather than dinner because Ellie has a school concert that evening, and Sunday, November 17, is the final meal in this calendar, but we have not picked a dish yet.

We also wrote down a few practical details under the dates. The person hosting checks whether there are enough plates and clean dish towels before the day. The cook does not have to pay for every ingredient alone, and people can ask the group to bring something simple, such as fruit or milk. If the meal is at Grandma Jo’s, we use the side entrance because the main stairwell door sticks, and the shopping bags should not be left in the hallway. If someone has a food allergy, they should tell the cook directly and also put it in the group message so the information does not get lost.

I corrected the phone entry, and Marcus checked that his chicken bowls were still on Monday, October 7. Grandma took a picture of the paper calendar and said she would call if the small print was hard to read. We agreed that any change needs a name and a date beside it rather than an erased note, and if the November 4 shift question is still unanswered by October 30, Lena will send a reminder in the group chat. We started the new watering rota at Cedar Lane Greenhouse on the first Monday in April, after the old clipboard went missing for two days. The house has three growing spaces: the warm house, the propagation tunnel, and the shaded potting bay. Each has a different set of needs, and the rota is meant to make those needs visible rather than make every person water the same number of minutes. Mara keeps the master sheet beside the handwashing sink and puts a small copy on the door of each space. The week runs Monday through Sunday, and whoever finishes a task initials the box and writes the time, not just a tick.

The warm house holds tomatoes, peppers, and two rows of basil. The tomatoes are in fabric bags, so their soil dries faster near the heater and slower under the north bench. On Monday and Thursday, the assigned person checks the first and last bags in each row with a finger before turning on the drip line. If either check is still damp, they water only the dry bags and note which row they skipped. The timer is set for six minutes, but that is a starting point, not a promise that six minutes will suit every bag. After a hot, bright afternoon, the soil can be dry by the following morning, but after a cloudy day the same setting can leave water pooled under the bags. Nobody should empty that pooled water until Mara has checked whether a blocked drain is causing it.

Jo waters Tuesday and Friday this month, and she showed the volunteers how to clear the little filter at the end of the line. She says, “Do not pull the black tube sideways because it can split at the join. If the filter is clogged, close the blue tap first, unscrew the cap over a bucket, rinse the mesh with clean water, and put the cap back without forcing it on. If the cap will not turn easily, stop and write that on the sheet.” The replacement caps are in a labelled tin in the office, but the old caps have a different thread, so the tin is not a general spare parts box. Right, when someone asks whether the short rinse matters, it does. The basil bed is fed from that same line, and grit from the filter can reduce the flow before anyone notices a wilted leaf.

The propagation tunnel has seed trays on the upper shelves and cuttings on the lower shelves. Those trays are not part of the warm house timer and should be checked by hand every morning except Sunday, when the person on duty can come after lunch. If the tunnel cover is shut and the air feels cool, they mist the cuttings lightly and leave the seed compost alone unless the surface is pale and beginning to crack. If the cover has been propped open for ventilation during the day, check the trays again before leaving because a breeze can dry the edges while the middle stays damp. On Wednesday—no, Thursday, I mean Thursday—the electrician is checking the fan, so Jo will keep the tunnel cover closed until the visit is over and then open it again if the thermometer is above twenty-six degrees.

The shaded potting bay contains the fern table, the young lemon trees, and a rack of empty pots. It gets less direct sun, but the roof gutter drips beside the west post during heavy rain, so do not assume the pots are dry just because the top looks dusty. Lift one pot from each end of the rack and feel its weight before watering. The ferns prefer steady moisture, but the lemon trees need their saucers emptied after watering. If rain is forecast the next day, skip the outdoor pots unless their roots are visibly dry, and write “rain check” beside the date. The weather board is updated at nine each morning by the first person through the gate. If nobody has updated it by then, use the greenhouse thermometer and look at the sky rather than guessing from yesterday’s note.

At the volunteer meeting, Ines asked if the leaf yellowing on the lemon trees meant we should add feed, and Jo said not yet because the newest leaves are green and the soil test from last week showed enough nutrients. The yellow leaves are on the shaded side and may be older leaves reaching the end of their cycle. Ines said, “Pois é, that makes sense,” and offered to turn the pots a quarter turn on Saturday so each side gets similar light. Turning them is fine, but do not move them closer to the glass because that strip gets cold at night. The blue plant labels belong to the lemon trees, and the white labels belong to the fern varieties. If a label has fallen out, place it flat on the bench beside the pot and tell Mara rather than guessing which plant it came from.

We agreed on a short handover note because several people only come in once a week. Write the date, the space, the check you made, and anything the next person needs to look at. For example: “Warm house, west row, bag four still damp at seven forty-five,” or “Tunnel, tray twelve, surface pale, misted lightly.” Do not write “fine” when you mean that you did not have time to inspect a space. If a scheduled person cannot come, they should message the group before nine so Mara can ask for cover. On Monday, she had to water the peppers after closing time because no one had seen the blank box and the soil had already begun to crack. Nobody was in trouble, but the late watering could have been avoided with a message and a clear handover.

1. If a hose is leaking, close its nearest tap and put the orange clip on the valve handle, then message Mara before using another hose.
2. If water is running across a path, put out the yellow floor sign and mop it before carrying trays through.
3. If a power strip or timer is wet, do not touch the plug. Switch off the room circuit at the marked panel and wait for Mara. The panel key hangs on the hook outside the office.
4. If leaves show a sudden change, photograph the plant beside its label and send the picture with the date and space. Do not spray a treatment or remove a whole plant on your own. The weekly rota can be adjusted, but the person changing it needs to tell everyone who is affected.

Yesterday, we found that the shaded bay hand sprayer had been filled with diluted soap for cleaning a pot and put back beside the plain water sprayer. I emptied it, rinsed it twice, and marked the handle with a green band so the two are easier to tell apart. Keep the soap sprayer on the lower shelf in the wash corner and use it only for pots. After cleaning, rinse the pot outside the fern area and return the sprayer with its nozzle loosened. The plain water sprayer stays on the central bench and is for misting cuttings only. If either bottle is empty, refill it from the labelled tap, not from the rain barrel, because the barrel can contain leaf debris.

The main condition for the first week is that if the night temperature is forecast below eight degrees, cover the lemon trees with fleece before the last person leaves and take the fleece off by ten the following morning, unless the temperature is still below eight degrees. In that case, leave it on and write a note for the next person. Do not cover the fern table because condensation gathers under the fleece and damages the new fronds. The fleece is folded in the grey basket under the potting bench, and the thermometer forecast is pinned next to the rota. Even if the forecast changes later, the note is useful because it tells us what was actually done and when.

On Sunday, Mara will count the watering cans and compare the rota with the initials and times before she puts up next week’s sheet. If a box is blank, she will ask the person who was assigned to it whether the check was missed or just not written down. She is not going to assume that an empty box means a plant was watered, and she is not going to mark a task complete for someone else. We also need to check that the two blue taps are fully closed and that the filter bucket has been emptied before the greenhouse is locked. The seed trays in the tunnel are still germinating unevenly, so keep checking each tray rather than treating them as one batch. If the west post gutter is dripping again, leave the fern pots where they are and add the location to the handover note.

Last Saturday, at the shared bicycle shed on Alder Lane, we held the first full residents’ meeting since the new key system went in in April. There were eleven people in the room, plus Jo from the housing office. The shed has twenty-four marked spaces and a narrow repair bench, but only eighteen spaces are assigned at the moment because six bikes have not been matched to an owner. Jo said the waiting list is still open and that nobody should move an untagged bike just because it looks abandoned. The meeting started at 6:15, and we had to finish before the caretaker locked the side gate at eight.

Mara brought the notebook from the entrance shelf and read out the complaints from May and June. The main concern was that the drain beside the west wall backed up during heavy rain and left a shallow pool under spaces seven through ten. Two residents said their rear tires had been sitting in water overnight, and one of them had replaced a chain after it rusted. Mara said the landlord had sent a plumber once, but the plumber cleared leaves only at the grate and did not inspect the pipe below. Jo has asked for another visit and will send us a date when the contractor confirms it. We agreed that residents can use the dry rack by the entrance for a wet bike, but should not block the fire route while the drain is being checked.

Then Omar explained the key log. He keeps a paper sheet in a plastic sleeve and records the date the key was borrowed, the space number, and the name of the borrower. He said a couple of people had written only their initials, so he could not tell who had the key when the side gate was found open on the ninth of June. He asked people to write their full first name and phone extension, if they have one. Mara said, “Right, that makes sense, but the older residents without a phone extension should not be asked to put a private number in a public notebook.” We decided the caretaker can confirm their names in person instead, and Jo will print a small note with that option.

We also talked about lights because the motion sensor over the repair bench switches off after about forty seconds. That is enough time to unlock a bike, but not enough to check a loose brake cable. Nico said he had tested the lamp at seven thirty on Monday, and it went dark while he was holding a wrench. “Er ist um halb acht gekommen” was the exact line he read from the message from his father, who sometimes helps with repairs. He explained that his father had arrived at half past seven, rather than that those words were a noise in the message. The electrician is due next Thursday and may be able to adjust the timer, but Jo has not promised that the visit will include a new light.

1. Keep the path to the side gate clear, even when the entrance rack is full.
2. Put a card with your name on a bike that is waiting for repair, and write the date you noticed the problem.
3. Do not use the red cabinet for oil or cleaning fluid because it belongs to the caretaker.
4. Tell Omar if a key is missing, but do not leave a spare key under the flowerpot by the gate. This was not a suggestion to hide it somewhere else; it is a reminder that the shed key is meant to stay with a resident or the caretaker.

Lina said, “Tá bom, I can bring labels on Friday,” and she meant yes, she will bring them, not that the meeting had ended.

After that, we checked the repair bench inventory. There are two hand pumps; one has a cracked gauge and still works if the user checks pressure with the small tire gauge. There are four tire levers, a patch kit with three patches left, a set of hex keys, and a floor brush. The adjustable wrench is missing, and nobody remembered taking it. Jo will ask the caretaker whether it was moved into the maintenance cupboard before we order another one. We also found a blue helmet with no name written inside and a child seat that has a loose buckle. Those items are on the top shelf and are not part of the free repair supplies until their owners come forward.

The condition that matters for the next meeting is the drain visit. If the contractor comes before the end of the month and confirms that the pipe is clear, we will ask Jo to put the remaining six spaces back on the assignment list. If the contractor cannot come or says the pipe needs more work, the spaces under the leak will stay unused, and we will ask for a written schedule before changing the list. Either way, nobody agreed to move a bike into those spaces first and ask permission later. Jo said she will update the residents by email, but anyone who does not use email can read the same note on the board beside the entrance.

We finished by discussing the Saturday repair morning on the twenty-second, from ten until noon. Mara can bring the sign-in sheet, and Nico can show people how to check brake pads, but he is not offering to adjust anyone’s brakes for them because the shed does not have a qualified mechanic. Lina will bring labels, and Omar will bring the key log. Jo asked us to tell her by Wednesday if we want the housing office to lend a folding table for the tools. She needs that answer before the caretaker prepares the room. The final note for the board should say that the repair morning is open to residents, that children need an adult with them, and that the side gate must remain clear throughout the session.
